title: A spiral disguised
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1032 seen edge-on, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1032 · constellation Cetus · about 100 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Like a wizard's staff set aglow, NGC 1032 cuts across the darkness of space in a narrow, bright stripe. It lies about a hundred million light-years away in the constellation Cetus, the Sea Monster.
The view hides the galaxy's true nature. NGC 1032 is a large spiral, but from Earth its broad disc of gas, dust and stars appears nearly edge-on, so it appears as a narrow stripe.

Several background galaxies are scattered around it. Many are face-on or tilted, showing their spiral arms and bright cores. Those angles reveal a lot about arms and nuclei, but to fully understand a galaxy's three-dimensional structure, astronomers also need an edge-on view like this one. It shows how stars are spread through the galaxy and lets astronomers measure the height of the disc and of the bright, star-filled core.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.63 x 2.87 arcminutes) and distance (100 million light years), the frame spans roughly 77,000 × 83,000 light-years. Its light set out about 100 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1032 in visible light through filters at 435 nm and 606 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, revealing the faint background galaxies around NGC 1032.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

alt: A thin, bright edge-on galaxy crossing the frame, with a few small spiral galaxies in the background.
